APX-000013.transcript:
Customer (David Kerr): I'm moving next week and need gas stopped at my old place and started at the new one.
Agent (Sipho Nkosi): Hi David Kerr, Sipho Nkosi here — let me pull that up.
Customer (David Kerr): What's the actual turnaround time between the stop and the start?
Agent (Sipho Nkosi): Sure. Let me get the account up.
Agent (Sipho Nkosi): Can you give me the account number from your bill, or the service address and the name on the account?
Customer (David Kerr): Yes, same address as always, and the account's under my name.
Customer (David Kerr): Do I need to be home for anyone to come out, or can this be done remotely?
Agent (Sipho Nkosi): What date do you need the stop to take effect?
Customer (David Kerr): The last day of the month. That's when we hand the keys back.
Agent (Sipho Nkosi): Is the new address in one of our service areas?
Customer (David Kerr): Yes, it's still in Leduc County.
Agent (Sipho Nkosi): Is the email on your account still current, for the confirmations?
Customer (David Kerr): It's an old one. Can you change it to my new email?
Agent (Sipho Nkosi): Let me take a look. I've processed the account request and confirmed the effective date against the service address change.
Agent (Sipho Nkosi): Okay, I've got it pulled up now.
Agent (Sipho Nkosi): A stop and start on the same day is routine. We read the old meter on the move-out date so you only pay to that day.
Agent (Sipho Nkosi): I've got the stop set for your move-out date and the start scheduled for your new address the same day, no technician visit needed for a standard meter transfer, and I've sent both confirmations to your email.
Customer (David Kerr): And the final bill for the old place?
Agent (Sipho Nkosi): It comes within two weeks of the move-out read.
Customer (David Kerr): Will the new account use the same payment details?
Agent (Sipho Nkosi): Yes, the pre-authorized payment moves over with you.
Agent (Sipho Nkosi): To recap: stop on the move-out date, start the same day at the new address, confirmations in your email.
Customer (David Kerr): Alright, thank you for looking into it.
Agent (Sipho Nkosi): Thanks for bearing with me — you're all set.

Agent Sipho Nkosi processed the account request and confirmed the effective date against the service address change. In the end, it was resolved on this interaction, and the customer rated it CSAT 5 (very satisfied).

APX-000038.transcript:
Customer (Robert Campbell): My bill jumped and I don't understand why. Did something change with my rate?
Agent (Vusi Molefe): Hi Robert Campbell, Vusi Molefe here — let me pull that up.
Customer (Robert Campbell): Is this the Phase 2 thing the AUC approved, or did I do something wrong on my account?
Agent (Vusi Molefe): Good question, a lot of customers are asking about this one. Let me check your account.
Agent (Vusi Molefe): Before I go into the account, can you confirm the service address and the account holder's name?
Customer (Robert Campbell): Sure, it's the house on the account, and the bill's in my name.
Customer (Robert Campbell): I've been on the same rate for years, why is this changing now?
Agent (Vusi Molefe): Roughly how much gas do you use in a year, or should I look it up?
Customer (Robert Campbell): No idea. Can you look it up?
Agent (Vusi Molefe): Did you get the letter by mail or by email?
Customer (Robert Campbell): By mail, a couple of weeks ago.
Agent (Vusi Molefe): Do you have any irrigation or shop meters on the same account?
Customer (Robert Campbell): No, just the house.
Agent (Vusi Molefe): Let me take a look. I've pulled up the account, confirmed the Rate 1/Rate 2 threshold under the August 1 Phase 2 restructuring, and walked through what changed on this specific account.
Agent (Vusi Molefe): Thanks for holding — I've got the full picture now.
Agent (Vusi Molefe): Since August 1, Rate 1 covers accounts using under 4,000 GJ a year and Rate 2 covers larger users. The AUC approved it as Phase 2 of the rate restructuring.
Customer (Robert Campbell): Okay. What's the actual next step here?
Agent (Vusi Molefe): Give me one more moment while I confirm the details.
Agent (Vusi Molefe): You're on Rate 1 since your annual usage is under 4,000 GJ, so the main change is the way the distribution charge is broken out on the bill — your total shouldn't move much. I've sent the AUC decision summary to your email so you have it on file.
Customer (Robert Campbell): So my total won't go up much?
Agent (Vusi Molefe): It shouldn't. Most of this month's jump is colder weather, not the rate change.
Customer (Robert Campbell): Can I get that in writing?
Agent (Vusi Molefe): The AUC summary and your usage figure are in your email now.
Agent (Vusi Molefe): To recap: you're staying on Rate 1, the change is mostly how the bill is laid out, and the summary is in your email.
Customer (Robert Campbell): Alright, thank you for looking into it.
Agent (Vusi Molefe): Thanks for bearing with me — you're all set.
APX-000038.narrative_summary: Robert Campbell, an Apex Utilities customer, contacted support on a rate-class change case. Agent Vusi Molefe pulled up the account, confirmed the Rate 1/Rate 2 threshold under the August 1 Phase 2 restructuring, and walked through what changed on this specific account. In the end, it was resolved on this interaction, and the customer rated it CSAT 4 (satisfied).

APX-000086.transcript:
Customer (Nicole Fraser): Why did my equalized payment change again? Nobody told me this was happening.
Agent (Kagiso Radebe): Hi Nicole Fraser, Kagiso Radebe here — let me pull that up.
Customer (Nicole Fraser): If the point of this plan is predictable payments, why does it keep moving?
Agent (Kagiso Radebe): Understood. Let me pull up the account and look at the charges before I say anything.
Agent (Kagiso Radebe): Can you give me the account number from your bill, or the service address and the name on the account?
Customer (Nicole Fraser): Yes, same address as always, and the account's under my name.
Customer (Nicole Fraser): This is the third time this year my equalized amount has changed on me.
Agent (Kagiso Radebe): When did you first join the equalization plan?
Customer (Nicole Fraser): About two years ago, when we moved in.
Agent (Kagiso Radebe): Did you get a notice before the amount changed?
Customer (Nicole Fraser): No. I found out when the payment came out.
Agent (Kagiso Radebe): Has anything changed at home, like a new appliance or more people?
Customer (Nicole Fraser): We had a baby, so the heat's been on more.
Agent (Kagiso Radebe): Let me take a look. I've reviewed the equalization plan's 12-month usage average and the reconciliation adjustment that triggered the change.
Agent (Kagiso Radebe): Alright, I can see exactly what's going on here.
Agent (Kagiso Radebe): The plan averages your last twelve months of usage and is reviewed at month six. If usage runs higher than the estimate, the difference is added.
Agent (Kagiso Radebe): The plan recalculates twice a year against your rolling usage average, and this adjustment reflects higher usage than last year's estimate — I've set up an email alert so you'll get advance notice before the next recalculation instead of finding out on the bill.
Customer (Nicole Fraser): Will it change again without warning?
Agent (Kagiso Radebe): The next review is in six months, and you'll get an email two weeks before it.
Agent (Kagiso Radebe): To recap: the catch-up is spread over the rest of the plan year, and you'll get an email two weeks before the next review.
Customer (Nicole Fraser): Alright, thank you for looking into it.
Agent (Kagiso Radebe): Thanks for bearing with me — you're all set.
APX-000086.narrative_summary: Nicole Fraser, an Apex Utilities customer, contacted support on a budget billing adjustment case. Agent Kagiso Radebe reviewed the equalization plan's 12-month usage average and the reconciliation adjustment that triggered the change. In the end, it was resolved on this interaction, and the customer rated it CSAT 5 (very satisfied).

Agent (Lerato Ndlovu): It comes within two weeks of the move-out read.
Customer (Karen Kerr): Will the new account use the same payment details?
Agent (Lerato Ndlovu): Yes, the pre-authorized payment moves over with you.
Agent (Lerato Ndlovu): To recap: stop on the move-out date, start the same day at the new address, confirmations in your email.
Customer (Karen Kerr): Alright, thank you for looking into it.

Customer (Susan Scott): Is the construction on my street part of the pipe replacement program, and how long will it last?
Agent (Sipho van der Merwe): Hi Susan Scott, Sipho van der Merwe here — let me pull that up.
Customer (Susan Scott): Who do I actually call if the crew damages something on my property?
Agent (Sipho van der Merwe): Thanks for letting us know. Let me check the project schedule for your street.
Agent (Sipho van der Merwe): Which street and block is the crew working on?
Customer (Susan Scott): Our block, the crew's been there since Monday.

Agent (Sipho van der Merwe): Do you need driveway access during the day?

Agent (Sipho van der Merwe): Is anyone at home who relies on the gas during the day?

Agent (Sipho van der Merwe): This is the pre-1975 pipe replacement work under our System Betterment Program — a notice with the timeline and a site contact number should have gone out two weeks ahead, I've resent it to your address and confirmed there's no planned service interruption.

Agent (Sipho van der Merwe): About two weeks on your block, with the road restored after.
Agent (Sipho van der Merwe): To recap: two weeks on your block, a door knock before any interruption, and the notice with the site contact is in your email.
Customer (Susan Scott): Alright, thank you for looking into it.

APX-000357.transcript:
Customer (Susan Wilson): I got a letter about a 'Rate 1' and 'Rate 2' change and I have no idea what it means for my bill.
Agent (Nomsa Khumalo): Hi Susan Wilson, Nomsa Khumalo here — let me pull that up.
Customer (Susan Wilson): Is this the Phase 2 thing the AUC approved, or did I do something wrong on my account?
Agent (Nomsa Khumalo): Good question, a lot of customers are asking about this one. Let me check your account.
Agent (Nomsa Khumalo): Before I go into the account, can you confirm the service address and the account holder's name?
Customer (Susan Wilson): Sure, it's the house on the account, and the bill's in my name.
Customer (Susan Wilson): I've been on the same rate for years, why is this changing now?
Agent (Nomsa Khumalo): Is this a home, a farm, or a business account?
Customer (Susan Wilson): It's our home. We're not a business.
Agent (Nomsa Khumalo): Did you get the letter by mail or by email?
Customer (Susan Wilson): By mail, a couple of weeks ago.
Agent (Nomsa Khumalo): Do you have any irrigation or shop meters on the same account?
Customer (Susan Wilson): No, just the house.
Agent (Nomsa Khumalo): Let me take a look. I've pulled up the account, confirmed the Rate 1/Rate 2 threshold under the August 1 Phase 2 restructuring, and walked through what changed on this specific account.
Agent (Nomsa Khumalo): Alright, I can see exactly what's going on here.
Agent (Nomsa Khumalo): Since August 1, Rate 1 covers accounts using under 4,000 GJ a year and Rate 2 covers larger users. The AUC approved it as Phase 2 of the rate restructuring.
Agent (Nomsa Khumalo): You're on Rate 1 since your annual usage is under 4,000 GJ, so the main change is the way the distribution charge is broken out on the bill — your total shouldn't move much. I've sent the AUC decision summary to your email so you have it on file.
Customer (Susan Wilson): So my total won't go up much?
Agent (Nomsa Khumalo): It shouldn't. Most of this month's jump is colder weather, not the rate change.
Agent (Nomsa Khumalo): To recap: you're staying on Rate 1, the change is mostly how the bill is laid out, and the summary is in your email.
Customer (Susan Wilson): Alright, thank you for looking into it.
Agent (Nomsa Khumalo): Thanks for bearing with me — you're all set.

APX-000377.transcript:
Customer (Kevin Grant): My bill jumped and I don't understand why. Did something change with my rate?
Agent (Karabo Zulu): Hi Kevin Grant, Karabo Zulu here — let me pull that up.
Customer (Kevin Grant): I've been on the same rate for years, why is this changing now?
Agent (Karabo Zulu): Good question, a lot of customers are asking about this one. Let me check your account.
Agent (Karabo Zulu): Can you give me the account number from your bill, or the service address and the name on the account?
Customer (Kevin Grant): Sure, it's the house on the account, and the bill's in my name.
Customer (Kevin Grant): Is this the Phase 2 thing the AUC approved, or did I do something wrong on my account?
Agent (Karabo Zulu): Is this a home, a farm, or a business account?
Customer (Kevin Grant): It's our home. We're not a business.
Agent (Karabo Zulu): Did you get the letter by mail or by email?
Customer (Kevin Grant): By mail, a couple of weeks ago.
Agent (Karabo Zulu): Do you have any irrigation or shop meters on the same account?
Customer (Kevin Grant): No, just the house.
Agent (Karabo Zulu): Let me take a look. I've pulled up the account, confirmed the Rate 1/Rate 2 threshold under the August 1 Phase 2 restructuring, and walked through what changed on this specific account.
Agent (Karabo Zulu): Alright, I can see exactly what's going on here.
Agent (Karabo Zulu): Since August 1, Rate 1 covers accounts using under 4,000 GJ a year and Rate 2 covers larger users. The AUC approved it as Phase 2 of the rate restructuring.
Agent (Karabo Zulu): Your annual usage is well under that, so you stay on Rate 1. What changed is how the distribution charge is shown on the bill.
Customer (Kevin Grant): Okay. What's the actual next step here?
Agent (Karabo Zulu): Give me one more moment while I confirm the details.
Agent (Karabo Zulu): Your usage puts you right at the edge of the new Rate 2 threshold, so this bill reflects the higher rate class — I don't have authority to move you back to Rate 1 manually, that's set by your metered usage under the AUC-approved structure.
Customer (Kevin Grant): Can't you just put me back on Rate 1?
Agent (Karabo Zulu): Not manually. The class follows your metered usage under the approved structure.
Customer (Kevin Grant): What happens if my usage drops next year?
Agent (Karabo Zulu): The class is reviewed against your annual usage, so it would move back if you fall under the threshold. I've noted that on the account.
Agent (Karabo Zulu): To recap, everything's noted on your file, and the team will follow up with you.
Customer (Kevin Grant): Alright, thank you for looking into it.
Agent (Karabo Zulu): Thanks for bearing with me — you're all set.

APX-000607.transcript:
Customer (Michael Duncan): Can you explain how the equalization plan works out my monthly amount?
Agent (Naledi Nkosi): Hi Michael Duncan, Naledi Nkosi here — let me pull that up.
Customer (Michael Duncan): If the point of this plan is predictable payments, why does it keep moving?
Agent (Naledi Nkosi): Understood. Let me pull up the account and look at the charges before I say anything.
Agent (Naledi Nkosi): Before I go into the account, can you confirm the service address and the account holder's name?
Customer (Michael Duncan): Sure, it's the house on the account, and the bill's in my name.
Customer (Michael Duncan): This is the third time this year my equalized amount has changed on me.
Agent (Naledi Nkosi): When did you first join the equalization plan?
Customer (Michael Duncan): About two years ago, when we moved in.
Agent (Naledi Nkosi): Has anything changed at home, like a new appliance or more people?
Customer (Michael Duncan): We had a baby, so the heat's been on more.
Agent (Naledi Nkosi): Would you rather stay on the plan or go back to regular billing?
Customer (Michael Duncan): Stay on it, if it stops jumping around.
Agent (Naledi Nkosi): Let me take a look. I've reviewed the equalization plan's 12-month usage average and the reconciliation adjustment that triggered the change.
Agent (Naledi Nkosi): Okay, I've got it pulled up now.
Agent (Naledi Nkosi): The plan averages your last twelve months of usage and is reviewed at month six. If usage runs higher than the estimate, the difference is added.
Customer (Michael Duncan): Okay. What's the actual next step here?
Agent (Naledi Nkosi): Give me one more moment while I confirm the details.
Agent (Naledi Nkosi): The plan recalculates twice a year against your rolling usage average, and this adjustment reflects higher usage than last year's estimate — I've set up an email alert so you'll get advance notice before the next recalculation instead of finding out on the bill.
Customer (Michael Duncan): Will it change again without warning?
Agent (Naledi Nkosi): The next review is in six months, and you'll get an email two weeks before it.
Customer (Michael Duncan): And the catch-up amount?
Agent (Naledi Nkosi): I've spread it over your remaining months so there's no lump sum.
Agent (Naledi Nkosi): To recap: the catch-up is spread over the rest of the plan year, and you'll get an email two weeks before the next review.
Customer (Michael Duncan): Alright, thank you for looking into it.
Agent (Naledi Nkosi): Thanks for bearing with me — you're all set.

Customer (Susan Murray): I'm following up again — there's a crew digging up the street outside my house and I never got any notice about it.

Agent (Lerato Ndlovu): I'm sorry about that — let me look at what happened last time and pick up from there.
Customer (Sarah Ross): If the estimate is wrong, how does the correction actually happen on a future bill?
Agent (Lerato Ndlovu): Thanks for bearing with us on this. Let me go through the bill with you properly.
Agent (Lerato Ndlovu): Can you give me the account number from your bill, or the service address and the name on the account?
Customer (Sarah Ross): Sure, it's the house on the account, and the bill's in my name.
Customer (Sarah Ross): Is there a way I can submit my own meter reading instead of waiting?
Agent (Lerato Ndlovu): Do you have a reading from the meter today?
Customer (Sarah Ross): I took a photo this morning. It's much lower than the bill.
Agent (Lerato Ndlovu): How many estimated bills have you had in a row?
Customer (Sarah Ross): Three, I think.
Agent (Lerato Ndlovu): Let me take a look. I've checked the meter-read schedule for the account and confirmed whether a self-read or field read was available.
Agent (Lerato Ndlovu): Okay, I've got it pulled up now.
Agent (Lerato Ndlovu): When our reader can't reach the meter, the bill is estimated from your past usage for the same months.
Agent (Lerato Ndlovu): Your meter is on the standard bi-monthly read cycle, so this cycle is estimated by design — I've noted your account for a field read next cycle, but I can't move today's estimate to an actual reading.
Customer (Sarah Ross): So this month's estimate just stands?
Agent (Lerato Ndlovu): For this cycle, yes. It corrects itself once there's an actual read.
Agent (Lerato Ndlovu): To recap: this estimate stands for now, a field read is booked for next cycle, and any difference is corrected on that bill.

Agent (Lerato Ndlovu): I've logged everything here so if this comes up again, the next agent has the full picture.

Customer (Robert Scott): I'm following up again — I need to dispute this bill. The fees on it don't make sense.
Agent (Sipho van der Merwe): Hi Robert Scott, Sipho van der Merwe here — let me pull that up.
Customer (Robert Scott): I already explained this on my last contact.
Agent (Sipho van der Merwe): I'm sorry about that — let me look at what happened last time and pick up from there.

Customer (Robert Scott): So there's nothing you can do?
Agent (Sipho van der Merwe): I can't waive a regulated charge. I can send the dispute to a billing specialist so every line is checked, not just explained.
Agent (Sipho van der Merwe): To recap: the regulated charges stand, a billing specialist is checking each line, and you'll hear back within five business days.

Customer (Megan Morrison): I'm following up again — I smell gas in my basement and I don't know what to do.
Agent (Naledi Nkosi): Hi Megan Morrison, Naledi Nkosi here — let me pull that up.
Customer (Megan Morrison): I already explained this on my last contact.
Agent (Naledi Nkosi): I'm sorry about that — let me look at what happened last time and pick up from there.
Customer (Megan Morrison): How long until someone actually gets here?
Agent (Naledi Nkosi): Okay. Stay calm, we're dealing with this now.
Agent (Naledi Nkosi): First, is everyone outside and away from the house? Then give me the address.
Customer (Megan Morrison): Yes, we're all out. The address is on the account.
Customer (Megan Morrison): Is it safe for me to stay in the house right now?
Agent (Naledi Nkosi): Is anyone in the house who couldn't get out?

Agent (Naledi Nkosi): Okay, I've got it pulled up now.
Agent (Naledi Nkosi): A technician is being sent now. Gas odour calls go straight to the front of the queue.

Customer (Megan Morrison): That's not really the answer I was hoping for, but okay.
Agent (Naledi Nkosi): I've logged everything here so if this comes up again, the next agent has the full picture.

Customer (Megan Martin): I'm following up again — my estimated bill was way higher than what I actually used last month.

APX-000803.transcript:
Customer (Chris Bell): I'm following up again — my bill is almost all fees and hardly any gas, and I want someone to explain it.
Agent (Kagiso Radebe): Hi Chris Bell, Kagiso Radebe here — let me pull that up.
Customer (Chris Bell): I already explained this on my last contact.
Agent (Kagiso Radebe): I'm sorry about that — let me look at what happened last time and pick up from there.
Customer (Chris Bell): I have used under CA$500 of actual gas and been charged thousands in fees — that math doesn't add up.
Agent (Kagiso Radebe): Thanks for bearing with us on this. Let me go through the bill with you properly.
Agent (Kagiso Radebe): Can you give me the account number from your bill, or the service address and the name on the account?
Customer (Chris Bell): Sure, it's the house on the account, and the bill's in my name.
Customer (Chris Bell): Every time I call about this I get a different answer and nobody sounds like they want to help.
Agent (Kagiso Radebe): Which bill are you looking at, this month's or the one before?
Customer (Chris Bell): This month's, but the last three have looked the same.
Agent (Kagiso Radebe): Do you have a figure in mind for what you think is wrong?
Customer (Chris Bell): I worked it out. Over two years it's a few hundred dollars of gas against thousands in charges.
Agent (Kagiso Radebe): Let me take a look. I've pulled the full fee breakdown against metered usage and reviewed the prior contact history on this dispute.
Agent (Kagiso Radebe): Okay, I've got it pulled up now.
Agent (Kagiso Radebe): The fixed daily charge and the distribution charge are set by the AUC for your rate class, so they apply even when usage is low.
Customer (Chris Bell): So is this actually getting fixed today?
Agent (Kagiso Radebe): I've confirmed the fee structure is billed correctly under the current rate schedule regardless of usage, and I don't have authority to waive charges that are applied correctly — I can escalate this to a billing specialist for further review.
Customer (Chris Bell): So I just keep paying fees on gas I don't use?
Agent (Kagiso Radebe): The regulated charges stay, yes. What I can do is have a billing specialist check every line, not just explain them again.
Agent (Kagiso Radebe): To recap: the regulated charges stand, a billing specialist is reviewing every line, and you'll get a call within five business days.
Customer (Chris Bell): That's not really the answer I was hoping for, but okay.
Agent (Kagiso Radebe): I've logged everything here so if this comes up again, the next agent has the full picture.
